Compile files and executable projects with the released compiler.

The release compiler directly emits supported programs. It does not invoke a C++
compiler, host C compiler, assembler, or linker.

## Compile a source file

```bash
hy check hello.hy
hy compile hello.hy -o hello
chmod +x hello
./hello
```

The default output is a standalone Linux x86-64 ELF executable. `check` finds
syntax and type errors; `compile` is the final authority because it also rejects
features the current backend cannot emit.

## Build a project

```bash
hy build app/App.hyproj -o app/bin/app
chmod +x app/bin/app
./app/bin/app
```

Executable project references contribute source files to one native compilation.
The current release does not produce library archives, build workspaces, resolve
packages, or run tests for you.

## Rebuild the compiler

Contributors can use a verified release binary as a seed to rebuild the compiler's
Hydrogen project closure. This is Hydrogen-only; a clean source-only checkout still
needs a trusted initial seed.

## Diagnostics and IR

```bash
hy check hello.hy --emit-ir
```

`check --emit-ir` prints bound executable IR for inspection; it does not create a
runnable debug executable. Failed `compile` and `build` commands return non-zero
and preserve an existing output artifact.

## UEFI output

```bash
hy compile uefi_hello.hy --target uefi-x64 -o BOOTX64.EFI
file BOOTX64.EFI
```

`BOOTX64.EFI` is firmware code, not a Linux executable. Put it on a FAT EFI
system partition or use the Australis ISO workflow, then boot it with UEFI
firmware or QEMU/OVMF.

The supported language surface and output targets in the current release.

Hydrogen releases ship the self-hosted Hydrogen compiler. This is the compiler you
use to write programs, build native applications, and build Australis OS. There is
no compiler choice in the normal user workflow.

The current release runs on Linux x86-64. Its default output is a standalone Linux
x86-64 executable. It can also emit the deliberately small `uefi-x64` firmware
proof used by Australis. Windows and macOS host executables are future ports.

## Supported language surface

| Area | Available now |
| --- | --- |
| Program structure | Namespaces, classes, public/private members, static and instance methods |
| Values | `int`, `byte`, `bool`, strings, arrays, enums, and `var` |
| Control flow | `if`, `while`, `break`, `continue`, and `return` |
| Objects | Constructors, instance fields, field initializers, and recursion |
| Linux services | Console output, file text/bytes, integer parsing, and managed allocation/GC |
| Projects | Executable `.hyproj` projects and source project references |
| UEFI proof | ASCII literals passed to `System.Console.WriteLine` in `Main` |

The current release does not yet implement `for`, inheritance, interfaces, struct
value semantics, generics, overloads, static fields, exceptions, pointers, manual
memory, a package manager, an interpreter, or editor tooling.

## Targets

```bash
# Linux-native executable
hy compile hello.hy -o hello

# Current UEFI console proof
hy compile hello.hy --target uefi-x64 -o BOOTX64.EFI
```

`uefi-x64` is not the Linux runtime in a different file format. It currently has
no general console API, file I/O, arguments, keyboard input, allocation API,
graphics API, or `Hydrogen.Uefi` library.

Download and use the self-hosted Hydrogen compiler on Linux x86-64.

Hydrogen is distributed as a self-hosted compiler binary. For normal language and
Australis development, download that release binary; you do not need the older
C++ SDK or a C++ compiler.

## Linux x86-64

Download the current Linux x86-64 asset from the
[Hydrogen compiler releases](https://github.com/Aurora-Softwares/Hylang-Compiler/releases),
extract it, and add its `bin` directory to your shell `PATH`. The release command
is named `hy`. (`.hy` remains the extension for Hydrogen source files.)

```bash
export PATH="/path/to/hydrogen-release/bin:$PATH"
hy tokens hello.hy
```

Add the same `PATH` entry to your shell profile (for example `~/.profile`) to make
`hy` available in new terminals. The next page compiles a first program and
confirms the release works.

```csharp
public class Program {

}
```

Compile and run it:

```bash

chmod +x hello

```

## Compile the EFI application

Create `uefi_hello.hy`:

```csharp
public class Program {
```

## Build and boot the Australis ISO

Install `mtools`, `xorriso`, QEMU, and OVMF, then use the companion repository:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Aurora-Softwares/Australis-OS.git
cd Australis-OS
make iso HYDROGEN="$(command -v hy)"
make run HYDROGEN="$(command -v hy)"
```

How the Hydrogen compiler reaches executable IR and native output.

> This is contributor documentation. To use Hydrogen, start with the released
> compiler in the Getting Started section.

The compiler parses Hydrogen source, binds names and types, lowers reachable
methods into executable IR, and emits native x86-64 output. The current Linux
backend includes its runtime in each executable; the UEFI path uses a deliberately
small PE32+ image builder for the firmware console proof.

The compiler's own CLI project is within the supported language subset, enabling a
verified Hydrogen binary to rebuild that project closure without a C++ toolchain.

Features outside the released subset must not be assumed to work merely because
older design material describes them. Extend the parser, checker, IR, backend, and
tests together when adding language features.

Native generations, UEFI proof output, and bootstrap boundaries.

> This is contributor documentation. Release users install `hydrogen-stage1` and
> do not need the historical C++ bootstrap to use Hydrogen.

The Hydrogen-written compiler emits standalone Linux x86-64 ELF executables by
default. It binds the complete source/reference closure of its CLI project and can
compile itself. It can additionally produce a constrained PE32+ UEFI console
application.

## UEFI proof target

The `uefi-x64` path is implemented in Hydrogen. It writes a minimal PE32+ EFI
image, provides an x86-64 EFI entry stub, encodes console text as UTF-16, and
calls the firmware text-output function through the UEFI system table. `mtools`
and `xorriso` package that executable into boot media; they do not compile it.

This is intentionally not a general ABI/runtime layer. It currently lowers the
console proof profile—ASCII literals passed to `System.Console.WriteLine` from the
static entry point. Managed heap support, firmware wrappers, keyboard support,
graphics, and general foreign-function calls are future work.

## Rebuild from a seed

Keep a verified compiler outside a new output directory, then rebuild the compiler
project with it:

```bash
"$HYDROGEN" build samples/self_hosting/Hydrogen.Compiler.Cli/Hydrogen.Compiler.Cli.hyproj \
  -o hydrogen-rebuilt
chmod +x hydrogen-rebuilt
```

A clean source-only checkout still needs a trusted initial seed. Repeated bootstrap
proofs build successive generations and verify their behavior and representative
artifacts.

## The current milestone

The released compiler runs on Linux x86-64 and directly emits standalone Linux
x86-64 executables. Its `uefi-x64` target can also create a bootable UEFI text
console Hello World. This is a real compiler-to-firmware milestone, but not yet a
complete UEFI library or an independent operating-system kernel.

Australis OS and native Australis applications are the primary direction. Linux
is the development host today; Windows and macOS compiler ports will follow when
they can be properly packaged and validated.
Control visibility with public and private members.

The released compiler supports public and private members.

Modifier Visibility
public Visible everywhere in the compilation
private Restricted to the declaring class

protected is not useful in the current release because inheritance is not yet supported. Static methods are supported; static fields are not.
Allocate, index, and share managed arrays.

The released compiler supports managed arrays of its supported element types.

Array counts must be int; void[] is invalid. Elements are zero/default initialized. Arrays are mutable reference types, so assignment and passing to a method retain the same underlying array. Out-of-range access is a runtime error.

Arrays may contain primitive values, strings, enums, and classes:

The current release has no built-in List<T>, map, set, or generic collection. Use arrays and explicit counters until the standard library provides them.
Branch, loop, continue, break, and return from Hydrogen methods.

The released compiler supports if, while, break, continue, and return. It does not support for; use a while loop with an explicit increment.

return; exits a void method. return expression; supplies a value from a non-void method. Exceptions are not part of the current release; use a status value or explicit condition for recoverable errors.

Enums are declared alongside classes at namespace scope:

Members without an explicit value begin at zero and increase by one. Enums can be fields, locals, parameters, return values, and array elements. Compare members of the same enum with == or !=. Console output formats an enum numerically, so select a string explicitly when human-readable output matters.
Use classes, fields, constructors, instance methods, and recursion.

Methods belong to classes. The released compiler supports static methods, instance methods, constructors, instance fields, parameters, return values, and recursion.

new Counter(10) allocates a managed reference object and invokes its constructor. Field initializers run before the constructor body. A class without a declared constructor has a parameterless default constructor. Fields start at zero, false, or null when not initialized.

Class assignment copies a reference, not an object. this refers to the current instance. Static methods have no this; pass an object explicitly to access its instance members.

The current release does not support overloads, inheritance, interfaces, structs, generic methods, or static fields.
Arithmetic, comparison, logical, unary, and string operators.

| Operator | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%` | Arithmetic; `+` also concatenates strings |
| `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` | Comparison |
| `&&`, `\|\|`, `!` | Logical AND, OR, and NOT |
| `-value` | Unary numeric negation |

```csharp
int remainder = 10 % 3;
bool inRange = remainder > 0 && remainder < 100;
string message = "Count: " + remainder;
```

`&&` and `||` short-circuit: the right-hand side is evaluated only when needed.
Compound assignment such as `+=` is not currently supported; write `i = i + 1`
instead.

Organize Hydrogen programs with namespaces, classes, and an entry point.

Hydrogen programs contain namespaces and types; executable statements belong inside methods. There are no top-level statements or free functions.

Namespaces use braces. A source can also declare a class in the global namespace.

Imports

Section titled “Imports”

Place imports before declarations. They let a file use simple names for types in that namespace but do not leak to other files. Use fully qualified builtin names, such as System.Console.WriteLine; this is the stable spelling recognized by the released compiler.

Entry point

Section titled “Entry point”

The released compiler accepts static Main methods returning void or int, with either no parameters or one string[] parameter. Project source files are listed in a .hyproj manifest; namespaces do not require a directory layout.
Core values, strings, arrays, null, and local type inference.

| Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `int` | Signed 64-bit integer |
| `byte` | Unsigned byte, useful for file contents |
| `bool` | `true` or `false` |
| `string` | Immutable managed byte string |
| `void` | A method returns no value |
| `T[]` | Mutable managed array |

Class instances are reference values. `null` is assignable to strings, classes,
and arrays. Accessing a null receiver is a runtime error. Enums provide named
numeric constants. The current release has no floating-point values or wider
integer types.

## Strings

```csharp
string message = "Count: " + 42 + ", active: " + true;
int size = message.Length;
string firstByte = message[0];
bool same = "hello" == "hel" + "lo";
```

`+` concatenates strings with strings, integers, and booleans. Equality compares
contents. Length and indexing work on bytes, not Unicode code points. Native
source literals support ASCII plus `\n`, `\r`, `\t`, `\\`, and `\"` escapes.

## Local inference

```csharp
var count = 42;
var text = "hello";
```

`var` is local type inference, not a dynamic type. It needs an initializer and is
not valid for parameters, fields, or method returns. The released compiler supports
classes and enums, not structs, interfaces, inheritance, or generics.

Australis-first language, firmware, kernel, and native-application direction.

Hydrogen's primary purpose is to build Australis OS and native Australis
applications. Linux is the current host and application target because it makes the
compiler practical to develop and validate today. Windows and macOS hosts are
valuable future ports, but they do not set the core work order.

## Completed foundation

- Hydrogen compiles its own compiler project closure.
- The default output is direct Linux x86-64 ELF.
- The self-hosted compiler emits a PE32+ `uefi-x64` application.
- Australis packages that output into a bootable ISO that displays Hydrogen text
  in QEMU/OVMF.

## Next: usable UEFI programs

The current firmware target is a console-output proof, not a runtime. The next
milestone is a minimal `Hydrogen.Uefi` library and the compiler support it needs:

- Console `Write`, `WriteLine`, and `Clear`.
- Keyboard input.
- Basic boot-service and memory-map wrappers.
- Explicit UEFI data layouts, function pointers, strings, and ABI support.
- Tests that compile and boot each feature.

This enables a firmware-hosted command shell written completely in Hydrogen.

## Then: Australis kernel work

1. Obtain the firmware memory map and call `ExitBootServices`.
2. Provide allocation and framebuffer output without firmware services.
3. Add interrupts plus keyboard and storage drivers.
4. Define the kernel/runtime boundary.
5. Grow userland and system calls.

## Native application platform

Hydrogen is intended to be the main language for native Australis applications,
not only for the kernel. Application libraries, process/system interfaces, and the
application model follow after the lower-level OS boundary is reliable.

Australis will eventually need its own coherent native visual system, in the broad
sense that Material and Liquid Glass give other platforms a visual language. That
work comes after input, rendering, windowing, and application-runtime foundations.

Console, file, conversion, and garbage-collection services in Linux-native output.

These services are implemented by the released compiler's Linux-native runtime.
Use the fully qualified names shown here.

| Call | Result | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `System.Console.Write(value)` | `void` | Print a string, integer, or boolean |
| `System.Console.WriteLine(value)` | `void` | Print a value followed by a newline |
| `System.IO.File.Exists(path)` | `bool` | Test a path |
| `System.IO.File.ReadAllText(path)` | `string` | Read a file as bytes in a string |
| `System.IO.File.ReadAllBytes(path)` | `byte[]` | Read a file into an array |
| `System.IO.File.WriteAllText(path, text)` | `void` | Create or replace a text file |
| `System.IO.File.WriteAllBytes(path, data)` | `void` | Create or replace a binary file |
| `System.Convert.ToInt32(text)` | `int` | Parse a signed decimal integer |

`ToInt32` returns Hydrogen's 64-bit `int`. Malformed/out-of-range values and failed
I/O terminate the application with an error. `WriteLine()` accepts no argument for
an empty line. `Console.ReadLine` is not implemented.

## GC diagnostics

| Call | Result | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `System.Runtime.GC.Collect()` | `void` | Force collection and release cached free pages |
| `System.Runtime.GC.GetAllocatedBytes()` | `int` | Active managed mapping bytes, excluding cached free pages |

## UEFI boundary

`--target uefi-x64` does not provide this Linux API table. It only emits
`System.Console.WriteLine` calls with ASCII literals from the static entry point.
It has no `Write`, files, conversion, GC, memory, or input support yet.

These services are implemented by the released compiler’s Linux-native runtime. Use the fully qualified names shown here.

Call Result Use
System.Console.Write(value) void Print a string, integer, or boolean

Managed values, the Linux-native runtime, and the UEFI target boundary.

Hydrogen programs use managed class objects, immutable byte strings, and mutable
arrays. Allocation and collection are automatic. Class and array assignment copy
references.

## Linux-native executables

The compiler embeds a Linux x86-64 runtime using raw Linux syscalls for console,
files, and memory mappings. It does not depend on libc, a C++ runtime, an assembler,
or a linker at application compilation time.

The heap uses a conservative, non-moving mark/sweep collector. Stack/register
values and heap payloads are scanned for allocation and interior pointers. Reachable
graphs and cycles are retained; unreachable mappings are reclaimed. Conservative
scanning can retain values that are no longer logically reachable.

Null access, out-of-range indices, malformed integers, failed I/O, and allocation
failure report errors and terminate with status `1`.

## UEFI output

The `uefi-x64` target has no embedded managed runtime. It is a small PE32+
firmware application that directly calls the UEFI text-console service for the
restricted Hello World profile.

Commands provided by the released self-hosted compiler.

The released compiler emits Linux x86-64 ELF executables by default and can emit
the constrained `uefi-x64` PE32+ EFI proof target.

```text
hy tokens <file.hy>
hy parse <file.hy>
hy check <file.hy|project.hyproj> [--emit-ir]
hy compile <file.hy> [--target uefi-x64] -o <output>
hy build <project.hyproj> -o <output>
hy stage-compare <project.hyproj> --stage1 <artifact> --stage2 <artifact>
```

`tokens` prints lexer tokens and source locations. `parse` prints a syntax outline.
`check` performs name and type checking; `--emit-ir` also prints typed operations.
`compile` handles one source file. `build` accepts a format-2 `type = "exe"`
project and follows `project_references` to library sources.

## Targets

Without `--target`, output is Linux x86-64 ELF with the native runtime.

`compile --target uefi-x64` emits a PE32+ EFI application. It currently supports
only the static-entry console proof: ASCII literals passed to
`System.Console.WriteLine`. There is no general runtime, object allocation, file
API, arguments, keyboard input, graphics support, or `Hydrogen.Uefi` library yet.

## Errors

Commands return `0` on success and `1` for invalid input or unsupported
compilation. A failed compilation does not create or overwrite the requested output.
An existing executable may therefore be from an earlier successful build.

Organize executable Hydrogen projects and source references.

A `.hyproj` manifest lists sources compiled together. Paths are relative to the
manifest, including referenced projects.

```text
Demo/
  App/App.hyproj
  App/Program.hy
  Math/Math.hyproj
  Math/Math.hy
```

`App/App.hyproj`:

```toml
format = 2
name = "App"
type = "exe"
sources = ["Program.hy"]
project_references = ["../Math/Math.hyproj"]
```

`Math/Math.hyproj`:

```toml
format = 2
name = "Math"
type = "lib"
sources = ["Math.hy"]
```

Build the executable project:

```bash
hy build Demo/App/App.hyproj -o Demo/app
chmod +x Demo/app
./Demo/app
```

Referenced libraries contribute sources to the final executable; they are not
separately linked artifacts. The released compiler does not build workspaces, test
projects, standalone library archives, packages, or dependency registries.
